row.cell: I know that: I've tried it. (a pause) Let's surround him, and give him a salute, one from here (pointing) and the other from here. (they station themselves: then, giving the signal to Libanus to chime in, loudly to Argyrippus) Good day, sir! (the lovers give a start) But—this lady you're hugging isn't smoke, is she?
Quidum?
Smoke? Why so?
620 Quia oculi sunt tibi lacrumantes, eo rogavi.
Well, your eyes are watering; that's why I asked.
Patronus qui vobis fuit futurus, perdidistis.
(tragically) You have lost a man who would have freed you and been your patron, my lads.
Equidem hercle nullum perdidi, ideo quia numquam ullum habui.
Lord! I haven't lost any such, no, indeed, seeing I never had any such.
Philaenium, salve.
Good day to you, Philaenium.
Dabunt di quae velitis vobis.
God grant all your wishes, to both of you.
Noctem tuam et vini cadum velim, si optata fiant.
I'd wish an evening with you and a cask of wine, if wishing was having.
Verbum cave faxis, verbero.
Hold your tongue, you rascal!
Tibi equidem, non mihi opto.
Oh, wish 'em for you, I mean, sir, not for myself.
Tum tu igitur loquere quod lubet.
Then in that case, say what you like.
Hunc hercle verberare.
Like? I'd like to give this chap (pointing to Leonida) a thrashing, by gad!

cell.p: Quisnam istuc adcredat tibi, cinaede calamistrate?
tun verberes, qui pro cibo habeas te verberari?

row.cell: (ironically) Well, well, who'd believe it of you, you frizzle-headed girl-hunter? You thrash me, you, you that live on thrashings?

cell.p: Ut vostrae fortunae meis praecedunt, Libane, longe,
qui hodie numquam ad vesperum vivam.

row.cell: (tragical again) Ah, Libanus, how far preferable your lot is to mine—I who will never never live till evening!
630 Quapropter, quaeso?
How's that, for mercy's sake?

cell.p: Quia ego hanc amo et haec me amat, huic quod dem nusquam quicquam est,
hinc med amantem ex aedibus eiecit huius mater.
argenti viginti minae me ad mortem appulerunt,
quas hodie adulescens Diabolus ipsi daturus dixit,
ut hanc ne quoquam mitteret nisi ad se hunc annum totum.
videtin viginti minae quid pollent quidve possunt?
ille qui illas perdit salvos est, ego qui non perdo pereo.

row.cell: Because I love her (indicating Philaenium) and she loves me, and (bitterly) never a penny can I find anywhere to give her; and her mother has thrown me out of the house here, me, her daughter's lover. I'm driven to my death by eighty pounds, eighty pounds young Diabolus promised to pay her to-day for letting no one else but him have my girl the whole of this next year. Do you see the power, the possibilities in eighty pounds? The man that loses them is saved. I don't lose them and I'm lost myself.
Iam dedit argentum?
Has he paid 'em over already?
Non dedit.
No.
Bono animo es, ne formida.
Cheer up; never you fear.
Secede huc, Libane, te volo.
Libanus! Come over here: I want you.
Si quid vis.
(obeying) Anything to please. (they withdraw and talk, heads close together)

cell.p: Obsecro vos
640 eadem istac opera suaviust complexos fabulari.

row.cell: (calling) For heaven's sake, you two! You'd find it pleasanter to hug each other, while you do your chatting!

cell.p: Non omnia eadem aeque omnibus, ere, suavia esse scito:
vobis est suave amantibus complexos fabulari,
ego complexum huius nil moror, meum autem hic aspernatur.
proinde istud facias ipse quod faciamus nobis suades.

row.cell: Tastes differ about what's pleasant, sir, let me tell you that. A fond pair like you find it pleasant to hug each other while you do your chatting; but, personally, I don't care for this fellow's hugs, and as for mine, he scorns 'em. So you go on and practise yourself what you preach to us.

cell.p: Ego vero, et quidem edepol lubens. interea, si videtur,
concedite istuc.

row.cell: Indeed I will, by Jove, yes, and gladly. Meanwhile you two go on and step aside there, if you see fit. (embraces Philaenium)
Vin erum deludi?
D'ye want to have some fun with master?
Dignust sane.
That I do, serves him right.
Vin faciam ut te Philaenium praesente hoc amplexetur?
D'ye want me to make Philaenium give you a squeeze right before his face?
Cupio hercle.
(enthusiastically) Gad, I long for one!
Sequere hac.
Come along. (leads the way back to Argyrippus and (Philaenium)
Ecquid est salutis? satis locuti.
Any good news? You have talked enough.

cell.p: Auscultate atque operam date et mea dicta devorate.
650 primum omnium servos tuos nos esse non negamus,
sed tibi si viginti minae argenti proferentur,
quo nos vocabis nomine?

row.cell: (importantly) Listen here, you two; pay attention and devour my remarks, (to Argyrippus) First of all, we are your slaves, we don't deny that; but if eighty pounds is produced for you, what will you call us?
Libertos.
(eagerly) Freedmen!
Non patronos?
Not patrons, eh?
Id potius.
Yes, yes, patrons!

cell.p: Viginti minae hic insunt in crumina,
has ego, si vis, tibi dabo.

row.cell: There's eighty pounds in this wallet here: I'll give it to you if you like.

cell.p: Di te servassint semper,
custos erilis, decus popli, thensaurus copiarum,
salus interioris24 corporis amorisque imperator.
hic pone, hic istam colloca cruminam in collo plane.

row.cell: Heaven prosper you for evermore, you guardian of your master, you glory of the populace, you storehouse of supplies, saviour of the inner man, and generalissimo of love! Put it here, hang that wallet here around my neck in plain sight.
Nolo ego te, qui erus sis, mihi onus istuc sustinere.
Let my master bear such a load? No sir, not I.
Quin tu labore liberas te atque istam imponis in me?
Why not take things easy yourself and let me stand the strain?
660 Ego baiulabo, tu, ut dacet dominum, ante me ito inanis.
I'll act as porter myself; as for you, you walk on ahead as a master should, empty handed.
Quid nunc?
(eagerly) Well now?
Quid est?
(drawling) Well what?
Quin tradis huc cruminam pressatum umerum?
Why don't you hand the wallet over and let it crush my shoulder?

cell.p: Hanc, cui daturu's hanc, iube petere atque orare mecum.
nam istuc proclive est, quo iubes me plane collocare.

row.cell: She's the one, (pointing to Philaenium) the one you'll give it to, tell her to ask me for it, tease me for it. You see that plain site you told me to put it on is a (with a sly glance at Philaenium) slope.

cell.p: Da, meus ocellus, mea rosa, mi anime, mea voluptas,
Leonida, argentum mihi, ne nos diiunge amantis.

row.cell: Oh, Leonida, you apple of my eye, my rosebud, my heart's delight, my darling, do give me the money! Don't separate us lovers.

cell.p: Dic me igitur tuom passerculum, gallinam, coturnicem,
agnellum haedillum me tuom die esse vel vitellum.
prehende auriculis, compara labella cum labellis.

row.cell: (with burlesque fondness) Well then, call me your little sparrow, hen, quail, call me your little lambkin, kidlet, or calfyboy, if you prefer: take hold of me by the earlaps and match my little lips to your little lips.
Ten osculetur, verbero?
She kiss you, you scoundrel?

cell.p: Quam vero indignum visum est?
670 at qui pol hodie non feres, ni genua confricantur.

row.cell: Yes, it does seem a shame, doesn't it? However, you don't get the cash this day, by gad, unless you rub my knees.
Quidvis egestas imperat: fricentur. dan quod oro?
"Need knows no shame." Rubbed they shall be. (gets down on ground, with poor grace, and clasps Leonida's knees) Won't you grant my prayer? (gets up)

cell.p: Age, mi Leonida, obsecro, fer amanti ero salutem,
redime istoc beneficio te ab hoc, et tibi eme hunc isto argento.

row.cell: Come, dear Leonida, please, please save your master that loves me so! Buy your freedom from him by this kindness, buy his favour for yourself with this money! (embraces him)

cell.p: Nimis bella es atque amabilis, et si hoc meum esset, hodie
namquam me orares quin darem. illum te orare meliust,
illic hanc mihi servandam dedit ei sane bella belle,
cape hoc sis, Libane.

row.cell: (leering at her) Ah, you're pretty, perfectly adorable: and if this belonged to me, I'd never let you tease me twice for it, never. But he's the one for you to tease: (pointing to Libanus) he gave it to me to keep for him. At him now, my pretty, prettily. Libanus, catch hold of this, will you! (tosses him the wallet)
Furcifer, etiam me delusisti?
What, you villain! Have you been making a fool of me?

cell.p: Numquam hercle facerem, genua ni tam nequiter fricares.
age sis tu in partem nunciam hunc delude atque amplexare hanc.

row.cell: Bless you, sir, I wouldn't, only you made such a bad job of rubbing my knees. (aside to Libanus) Come on now, will you; you take your turn at fooling him and cuddling her.
Taceas, me spectes.
(aside to Leonida) Shut up: you watch me!

cell.p: 680 Quin ad hunc, Philaenium, adgredimur,
virum quidem pol optimum et non simulem furis huius?

row.cell: (aside to Philaenium) Why not make up to him, Philaenium? He's a very decent sort, Libanus is, gad yes, nothing like this thief. (indicating Leonida)
Inambulandum est: nunc mihi vicissam supplicabunt.
(aside as they approach) Now for some strutting around: here's where I come in for being supplicated. (parades magnificently back and forth)

cell.p: Quaeso hercle, Libane, sis erum tuis factis sospitari,
da mihi istas viginti minas. vides me amantem egere.

row.cell: Hang it all, Libanus, for mercy's sake be a good fellow and save your master's life! Give me that eighty pounds. You see I'm in love and need the money.

cell.p: Videbitur. factum volo. redito huc contemno
nunc istanc tantisper iube petere atque orare
mecum.

row.cell: We'll see about it. Happy if I can oblige. Come back early in the evening. Meanwhile now just tell the lady there to ask me for it and tease me for it.
Amandone exorarier vis ted an osculando?
Tease it from you by loving you, or by kissing you, which?
Enim vero utrumque.
Oh well, try both of 'em.
Ergo, obsecro, et tu utrumque nostrum serva.
(fondling him) And both of us, then,—do rescue us, please, please!

cell.p: O Libane, mi patrone, mi trade istuc. magis decorumst
690 libertum potius quam patronum onus in via portare.

row.cell: O Libanus, my dear patron, do hand it over to me! A freedman is the proper person to carry a load on the street, not his patron.

cell.p: Mi Libane, ocellus aureus, donum decusque amoris,
amabo, faciam quod voles, da istuc argentum nobis.

row.cell: My own Libanus, my little golden treasure boy, love's gift and glory, oh, I'll adore you, do anything for you, only give us that money!

cell.p: Dic igitur med aniticulam, columbam vel catellum,
hirundinem, monerulam, passerculum putillum,
fac proserpentem bestiam me, duplicem ut habeam linguam,
circumda torquem bracchiis, meum collum circumplecte.

row.cell: Then call me your little ducky, dovey, doggieboy, your swallow, your little jackdaw, your little tootsie wootsie sparrowkin: (opening his mouth) make a reptile of me and let me have a double tongue in my mouth; throw a chain of arms around me; clasp me close around my neck.
Ten complectatur, carnufex?
Put her arms around you, you gallows-bird!

cell.p: Quam vero indignus videor?
ne istuc nequiquam dixeris tam indignum dictum in me,
vehes pol hodie me, si quidem hoc argentum ferre speres.

row.cell: An awful shame, isn't it, really now? Not to have you saying such shameful things of me free of charge, you'll carry me on your back to-day, by gad, that is, if you count on getting this cash.
Ten ego veham?
I carry you on my back—I?
700 Tun hoc feras argentum aliter a me?
See any other way of getting this cash, do you—you?

cell.p: Perii hercle. si verum quidem et decorum erum vehere servom,
inscende.

row.cell: O damnation! Well, if it is right and proper for a master to carry a servant on his back—get up.

cell.p: Sic isti solent superbi subdomari.
asta igitur, ut consuetus es puer olim scin ut dicam?
em sic. abi, laudo, nec te equo magis est equos ullus sapiens.

row.cell: Here's how those toplofty ones are tamified. Now then, stand by—the way you used to do years ago as a boy. Know how I mean? (Argyrippus sidles up and bends over) There! That's it! Good for you! Capital! There isn't a more knowing bit of horse-flesh than you anywhere.
Inscende actutum.
Get up, and be quick about it!

cell.p: Ego fecero hem quid istuc est? ut tu incedis?
demam hercle iam de hordeo, tolutim ni badizas.

row.cell: (springing on his shoulders) So I will. (Argyrippus moves off slowly) Hullo! What's the matter? How you do jog along! By gad, I'll dock your barley directly, if you don't stir yourself and gallop. (Argyrippus gallops)
Amabo, Libane, iam sat est.
There's a good fellow, Libanus,—that's enough now!

cell.p: Numquam hercle hodie exorabis
nam iam calcari quadrupedo agitabo advorsum clivom,
postidea ad pistores dabo, ut ibi cruciere currens.
710 asta ut descendam nunciam in proclivi, quamquam nequam es.

row.cell: Not on your life—you don't beg off this day. Why, now I'm going to dig the spurs in and trot you up a hill: afterwards I'll hand you over to the millers to do some running for 'em at the end of a rawhide. Stand still! so that I can dismount on the slope now, even though you are a good-for-nothing beast. (gets off)

cell.p: Quid nunc, amabo? quoniam, ut est libitum, nos delusistis,
datisne argentum?

row.cell: How about it now? There's a good fellow! Seeing you two have had your fill of sport with me, going to give us the money, are you?

cell.p: Si quidem mihi statuam et aram statuis
atque ut deo mi hic immolas bovem: nam ego tibi Salus sum.

row.cell: Oh well, if you put me up an altar and statue, yes, and offer me up an ox here the same as a god: for I'm your goddess Salvation, I am.

cell.p: Etiam tu, ere, istunc amoves abs te atque25 ipse me adgredere
atque illa, sibi quae hic iusserat, mihi statuis supplicasque?

row.cell: Come, sir, get rid of that chap, won't you, and apply to me in person, yes, and let me have those statues and supplications he ordered for himself.
Quem te autem divom nominem?
Ah, and by what name does your godship pass?
Fortunam, atque Obsequentem.
Fortune, yes sir, Indulgent Fortune.
Iam istoc es melior.
Now there's where you are better.
An quid est homini Salute melius?
Eh? what's better for a man than Salvation?
Licet laudem Fortunam, tamen ut ne Salutem culpem.
I can praise Fortune and still not disparage Salvation.
Ecastor ambae sunt bonae.
Mercy me, they're both good.
Sciam ubi boni quid dederint.
I'll know so when I get something good out of them.
Opta id quod ut contingat tibi vis.
Wish for something you want to happen to you.
Quid si optaro?
What if I do?
720 Eveniet.
It'll come true.
Opto annum hunc perpetuom mihi huius operas.
My wish is to have this lady's attentions this whole next year through.
Impetrasti.
You've got it.
Ain vero?
Really? really?
Certe inquam.
Sure thing I tell you.

cell.p: Ad me adi vicissim atque experire.
exopta id quod vis maxime tibi evenire: fiet.

row.cell: It's my turn—come over here and give me a trial. Long for something you most want to come true: it will.

cell.p: Quid ego aliud exoptem amplius nisi illud cuius inopiast,
viginti argenti commodas minas, huius quas dem matri.

row.cell: What could I long for more than something I haven't got a trace of—a round eighty pounds to give this girl's mother?
Dabuntur, animo sis bono face, exoptata optingent.
Forthcoming. Keep your courage up: your longing will be gratified.
Ut consuevere, homines Salus frustratur et Fortuna.
(incredulous) Salvation is at her old tricks, fooling people, and Fortune too.
Ego caput huic argento fui hodie reperiundo.
In lighting on this cash to-day—I'm the one that's been the head of it!
Ego pes fui.
I'm the one that's been the foot of it!

cell.p: Quin nec caput nec pes sermoni apparet.
730 nec quid dicatis scire nec me cur ludatis possum.

row.cell: And upon my soul, your discourse is a puzzle from head to foot. I can't understand your talk, or why you're making game of me.

cell.p: Satis iam delusum censeo. nunc rem ut est eloquamur.
animum. Argyrippe, advorte sis. pater nos ferre hoc iussit
argentum ad ted.

row.cell: (aside to Leonida) I move he's been fooled with long enough. Come on, let's out with it. (to Argyrippus) Your kind attention, Argyrippus! Your father told us to bring this money to you. (holding up wallet)
Ut temperi opportuneque attulistis.
Oh, you've brought it just in time, just at the right moment!

cell.p: Hic inerunt viginti minae bonae, mala opera partae;
has tibi nos pactis legibus dare iussit.

row.cell: You'll find in here eighty good sovereigns ill-gotten: he said to give 'em to you according to terms agreed upon.
Quid id est, quaeso?
Terms? What terms, for mercy's sake?
Noctem huius et cenam sibi ut dares.
That you're to give him an evening with this lady, and a dinner.

cell.p: Iube advenire quaeso:
meritissimo eius quae volet faciemus, qui hosce amores
nostros dispulsos compulit.

row.cell: Tell him to come along, yes, yes! We'll do what he wants, and quite right we should, after the way he's gathered our scattered love to the fold. (takes wallet from Libanus)

cell.p: Patierin, Argyrippe,
patrem hanc amplexari tuom?

row.cell: Going to put up with your father's hugging her, are you, Argyrippus?

cell.p: Haec faciet facile ut patiar
740 Leonida, curre obsecro, patrem huc orato ut veniat.

row.cell: (waving wallet) This will easily enable me to put up with it. Leonida, for heaven's sake run and beg my father to come here.
Iam dudum est intus.
(pointing to Cleareta's house) He was in there long ago.
Hac quidem non venit.
He certainly didn't come this way.

cell.p: Angiporto
illac per hortum circum ut clam, ne quis se videret.
huc ire familiarium: ne uxor resciscat metuit
de argento si mater tua sciat ut sit factum—

row.cell: Sneaked in by the alley there through the garden, so that none of the servants would see him enter: he's afraid of his wife finding out. If your mother was to learn about the money, how it was—

cell.p: Heia,
bene dicite.

row.cell: Hold on there! No ominous remarks!
Ite intro cito.
In with you, quick!
Valete.
Good-bye, you two.
Et vos amate.

And spoon away, you two.
[exeunt Argyrippus and Philaenium into Cleareta's house,Libanus and Leonida into house of Demaenetus.
ACTVS IV
ACT IV
enter Diabolus and Parasite.

cell.p: Agedum istum ostende quem conscripsti syngraphum
inter me et amicam et lenam. leges pellege
nam tu poeta es prorsus ad eam rem unicus.

row.cell: Come on, show me that contract you drew up between me and my mistress and the Madame. Read over the terms. Ah, you're the one and only artist at this business.
Horrescet faxo lena, leges cum audiet.
(producing a document) I warrant you Madame will shudder when she hears the terms.
Age quaeso mi hercle translege.
Come come, man, for the Lord's sake let's have 'em!
Audin?
Are you listening?
750 Audio.
Yes.

cell.p: "Diabolus Glauci filius Clearetae
lenae dedit dono argenti viginti minas,
Philaenium ut secum esset noctes et dies
hunc annum totum."

row.cell: (reading) "Diabolus, son of Glaucus, has given to Cleareta, Madame, a present of eighty pounds to the end that Philaenium throughout the coming year may spend her nights and days with him."
Neque cum quiquam alio quidem.
Yes, and not with anyone else, either.
Addone?
Shall I add that?
Adde, et scribas vide plane et probe.
Add that, and see you put it down in a good firm hand.

cell.p: "Alienum hominem intro mittat neminem.
quod illa aut amicum aut patronum nominet,
aut quod illa amicae26 amatorem praedicet,
fores occlusae omnibus sint nisi tibi.
760 in foribus scribat occupatam esse se.

row.cell: (after doing so) "She is to admit no male outsider into her house. In case she call him a mere friend or guardian, or in case she allege him to be the lover of a friend of hers, her doors must be closed to all but you. She must post a notice on the doors stating that she is engaged.

cell.p: aut quod illa dicat peregre allatam epistulam,
ne epistula quidem ulla sit in aedibus
nec cerata adeo tabula; et si qua inutilis
pictura sit, eam vendat: ni in quadriduo
abalienarit, quo abs te argentum acceperit,
tuos arbitratus sit, comburas, si velis,
ne illi sit cera, ubi facere possit litteras.

row.cell: Or in case she say that a letter from foreign parts has been delivered to her, there must be no letter at all in the house, nor so much as a waxen tablet; and if there be any undesirable picture about, let her sell it: unless she shall have removed it within four days after receipt of your money, it shall be at your disposal: you may burn it up, if you deem fit, that she may have no wax whereon to write.

cell.p: vocet convivam neminem illa, tu voces;
ad eorum ne quem oculos adiciat suos.
770 si quem alium aspexit, caeca continue siet.
tecum una potet, aeque pocla potitet:
abs ted accipiat, tibi propinet, tu bibas,
ne illa minus aut plus quam tu sapiat."

row.cell: She must invite no guest to the house: you shall invite them; and she must have eyes for none of them. If her glance has fallen on another man, she must become blind forthwith. She must drink with you only, and drink with you glass for glass: let her receive the glass from your hands, drink to your health, and then do you take it and drink, so that she may have no—(unobtrusively dropping the aspirate) whit more than you, nor less."
Satis placet.
(not noticing) Quite satisfactory.

cell.p: "Suspiciones omnes ab se segreget.
neque illaec ulli pede pedem homini premat,
cum surgat, neque cum in lectum inscendat proximum,
neque cum descendat inde, det cuiquam manum:
spectandum ne cui anulum det neque roget.
talos ne cuiquam homini admoveat nisi tibi.
780 cum iaciat, 'te' ne dicat: nomen nominet.

row.cell: "She must keep herself above every suspicion. She must not touch feet with any man when she arises from table: and when she steps upon the adjoining couch, or steps down therefrom, she must take no one's hand. She must give no one her ring to look at, nor ask to look at his. To no man save yourself must she pass the dice. On making a throw she must not say, 'TheeE I invoke!' She is to name your name.

cell.p: deam invocet sibi quam libebit propitiam,
deum nullum; si magis religiosa fuerit,
tibi dicat: tu pro illa ores ut sit propitius.
neque illa ulli homini nutet, nictet, annuat.
post, si lucerna exstincta sit, ne quid sui
membri commoveat quicquam in tenebris."

row.cell: Let her call upon any goddess she pleases for favour, but upon no god; if she have religious scruples in regard to this, let her tell you, and do you make the prayer for his favour in her stead. To no man shall she nod, wink, or signify compliance. Further, if the lamp go out, she is not to move a single limb in the darkness."

cell.p: Optumest.
ita scilicet facturam. verum in cubiculo—
deme istuc—equidem illam moveri gestio.
nolo illam habere causam et votitam dicere.

row.cell: Excellent! To be sure she mustn't, (pause) But in our own room—cut that clause out—why, I'm keen as can be for her to be lively there! I don't want her to have an excuse and say the contract forbids.
Scio, captiones metuis.
I see, you fear some catch.
Verum.
Exactly.

cell.p: 790 Ergo ut iubes
tollam.

row.cell: Well then, I shall strike that out, as you order.
Quid ni?
Of course you will.
Audi relicua.
Listen to the rest.
Loquere, audio.
Go on: I am listening.

cell.p: "Neque ullum verbum faciat perplexabile,
neque ulla lingua sciat loqui nisi Attica,
forte si tussire occepsit, ne sic tussiat,
ut cuiquam linguam in tussiendo proserat.
quod illa autem simulet, quasi gravedo profluat,
hoc ne sic faciat: tu labellum abstergeas
potius quam cuiquam savium faciat palam.

row.cell: "She must use no phrase of double meaning, and must know how to speak no language but the Attic. If she should happen to cough, she is not to cough so, (illustrating) in such a way as to extend her tongue toward anyone. Moreover, in case she pretends to have a running cold, she must not do this: (purses his lips) you are to wipe her little lip yourself rather than let her pucker up her mouth for anyone so obviously.

cell.p: nec mater lena ad vinum accedat interim,
800 nec ulli verbo male dicat. si dixerit,
haec multa ei esto, vino viginti dies
ut careat."

row.cell: Nor shall the Madame, her mother, drop in while you are having your wine, or say a single abusive word to anyone. If such a word be said by her, the penalty shall be this—no wine for her for twenty days."
Pulchre scripsti. scitum syngraphum.
Splendid document! Capital contract!

cell.p: "Tum si coronas, serta, unguenta iusserit
ancillam ferre Veneri aut Cupidini,
tuos servos servet, Venerine eas det an viro.
800 si forte pure velle habere dixerit,
tot noctes reddat spurcas quot pure habuerit."
haec sunt non nugae, non enim mortualia.

row.cell: "Then if she bid her maid carry chaplets, wreaths, perfumes to Venus or to Cupid, your servant shall observe whether she gives them to Venus, or to a man. Should she happen to express a wish for religious seclusion, she must give you as many hours of love as she has of loneliness." These be no trifles; these be no dirges for dead folk, I tell you. The terms are highly satisfactory. Follow me in.
Placent profecto leges, sequere intro.
Very well.
Sequor.
[exeunt into Cleareta's house: sound of wrangling within: re-enter Diabolus and Parasite from house.
IV. 2.
Scene 2.

cell.p: 810 Sequere hac, egone haec patiar aut taceam? emori
me malim, quam haec non eius uxori indicem.
ain tu? apud amicam munus adulescentuli
fungare, uxori excuses te et dicas senem?
praeripias scortum amanti atque argentum obicias
lenae? suppiles clam domi uxorem tuam?

row.cell: (incensed) Come along! I put up with this? I hold my tongue? I'd rather perish from the earth than not let it out to his wife! (shouting to Demaenetus within) You will, will you? You will play the gay young spark with a mistress and excuse yourself to your wife on the plea of old age, eh? You will snatch a girl from her lover and toss your money to the Madame, eh? You will filch things from your lady at home on the sly, eh?

cell.p: suspendam potius me, quam tu haec tacita auferas.
iam quidem hercle ad illam hinc ibo, quam tu propediem,
nisi quidem illa ante occupassit te, effliges scio,
luxuriae sumptus suppeditare ut possies.

row.cell: I'd sooner hang myself than let you carry it off so and nothing said. By the Lord, I'll go to her this very minute, I will, the woman you're bound to bring to pauperism shortly,—if she doesn't forestall you, that is,—just so that you may be kept in funds for your orgies!

cell.p: 820 Ego sic faciundum censeo: me honestiust,
quam te palam hanc rem facere, ne illa existimet
amoris causa percitum id fecisse te
magis quam sua causa.

row.cell: (calmly, judiciously) In my opinion, this is the way we should handle the case: it would look better for me to appear in the matter than you; she might think you were hard hit and did it more out of jealousy than out of regard for her.

cell.p: At pol qui dixti rectius.
tu ergo fac ut illi turbas lites concias;
cum suo sibi gnato unam ad amicam de die
potare, illam expilare narra.

row.cell: Right you are, gad yes, that is better! Then raise hell for him yourself; stir up a row; notify her that he's having a daylight carouse with his own son, one girl between 'em there at her house, and she herself being rooked for it!

cell.p: Ne mone,
ego istud curabo.

row.cell: No advice needed! I shall take care of that.
(827) At ego te opperiar domi.27

Well, I'll wait for you at home.27
[exit.
ACTVS V
ACT V
the door of Cleareta's house is open, showing Argyrippus, Demaenetus, and Philaenium banqueting, Philaenium being on a couch beside Demaenetus and trying not to seem bored by his gallantries.
830 Numquidnam tibi molestumst, gnate mi, si haec nunc mecum accubat?
You don't mind it, do you, my boy,—her being on the couch here with me? (merrily chucks Philaenium under the chin)

cell.p: Pietas, pater, oculis dolorem prohibet. quamquam ego istanc amo,
possum equidem inducere animum, ne aegre patiar quia tecum accubat.

row.cell: (dolefully) My duty as a son takes the sting out of the sight, father. Even though I do love her, of course I can persuade myself not to be disturbed at her being with you.
Decet verecundum esse adulescentem, Argyrippe.
A young fellow should be modest, Argyrippus.

cell.p: Edepol, pater,
merito tuo facere possum.

row.cell: Ah yes, father, I can behave as you deserve.

cell.p: Age ergo, hoc agitemus convivium
vino et28 sermoni suavi. nolo ego metui, amari mavolo,
mi gnate, me abs te.

row.cell: (jovially) Come on then, let's have a lively banquet—wine and sweet converse, my dears! None of your filial awe for me: your love is what I want, my lad.
Pol ego utrumque facio, ut aequom est filium.
(still more dolefully) Ah yes, father, I give you both, as a son should.
Credam istuc, si esse te hilarum videro.
I'll believe that, once I see you looking jolly.
An tu me tristem putas?
(with a deep sigh) You don't think I'm ... melancholy ... do you?
Putem ego, quem videam aeque esse maestum ut quasi dies si dicta sit?
Think so? When you look as sepulchral as if you were docketed for trial!
Ne dixis istuc.
Don't say that.
839, 840 Ne sic fueris: ilico ego non dixero.
Don't be that, and I'll stop saying it soon enough.
Em aspecta: rideo.
(making a dismal effort to look happy) Here now! See! I'm smiling.
Utinam male qui mihi volunt sic rideant.
(dryly) I wish my enemies were blessed with a smile like that.

cell.p: Scio equidem quam ob rem me, pater, tu tristem credas nunc tibi:
quia istaec est tecum. atque ego quidem hercle ut verum tibi dicam. pater,
ea res me male habet; at non eo, quia tibi non cupiam quae velis;
verum istam amo. aliam tecum esse equidem facile possum perpeti.

row.cell: Of course I know why you think my bearing toward you now is melancholy, father,—because she's with you. And good heavens, father, to tell you the truth, I—it does make me miserable; not because I'm not eager to have your wishes gratified; but I love that girl. If it was some other one, I shouldn't mind at all, really I shouldn't.
At ego hanc volo.
I want this one, though.
Ergo sunt quae exoptas: mihi quae ego exoptem volo.
Well then, you've got your desire: I wish I could have the same luck!

cell.p: Unum hunc diem perpetere, quoniam tibi potestatem dedi,
cum hac annum ut esses, atque amanti argenti feci copiam.

row.cell: Oh, you'll take it calmly this one day, now that I've given you the chance to be with her for a year, and furnished forth my young gallant with funds.
Em istoc me facto tibi devinxti.
Just the point! You have me bound hard and fast by that.
849, 850 Quin te ergo hilarum das mihi?
Come then, surrender and be jolly, won't you?
Scene 2.
enter Artemona and Parasite from house of Demaenetus.

cell.p: Ain tu meum virum his potare, obsecro, cum filio
et ad amicam detulisse argenti viginti minas
meoque filio sciente id facere flagitium patrem?

row.cell: (tempestuously) What's that, for heaven's sake,—my husband carousing here with his son, and brought eighty pounds to a mistress, and my son conniving at such an outrage on the part of his father, his father?

cell.p: Neque divini neque mi humani posthac quicquam accreduas,
Artemona, si huius rei me esse mendacem inveneris.

row.cell: Never trust me in another thing divine or human, madam, if you find I have misinformed you in this.

cell.p: At scelesta ego praeter alios meum virum29 frugi rata,
siccum, frugi, continentem, amantem uxoris maxume.

row.cell: But oh dear me! I thought my husband was the very paragon of men, a sober man, a worthy, moral man that loved his wife devotedly.

cell.p: At nunc dehinc scito illum ante omnes minimi mortalem preti,
madidum, nihili, incontinentem atque osorem uxoris suae.

row.cell: But from now on you must realize that he is the very scum of the earth, a toping man, a worthless, immoral man that hates the wife of his bosom.
860 Pol ni istaec vera essent, numquam faceret ea quae nunc facit.
Mercy yes! unless all that was true, he would never be acting as he does now.

cell.p: Ego quoque hercle illum antehac hominem semper sum frugi ratus,
verum hoc facto sese ostendit, qui quidem cum filio
potet una atque una amicam ductet, decrepitus senex.

row.cell: I always thought he was a worthy man myself before to-day, upon my soul I did: but now he shows himself in his true colours—carousing with his own son and sharing his mistress with him, the old ruin!

cell.p: Hoc ecastor est quod ille it ad cenam cottidie.
ait sese ire ad Archidemum, Chaeream, Chaerestratum,
Cliniam, Chremem, Cratinum, Diniam, Demosthenem:
is apud scortum corruptelae est liberis, lustris studet.

row.cell: Good gracious! This explains his going out to dinner every day! He with his tales of going to dine with Archidemus, Chaerea, Chaerestratus, Clinia, Chremes, Cratinus, Dinias, Demosthenes—and all the time corrupting his children at a harlot's, haunting houses of ill fame!
Quin tu illum iubes ancillas rapere sublimen domum?
Why not tell your maids to pick him up and take him off home?
Tace modo. ne ego illum ecastor miserum habebo.
You just keep still. Oh, but I'll make life miserable for him, I swear I will!

cell.p: Ego istuc scio,
ita fore illi dum quidem cum illo nupta eris.

row.cell: I have no doubt about that, just as long as he is your husband.

cell.p: 870 Ego censeo.
eum30 etiam hominem in senatu dare operam aut clientibus,
ibi labore delassatum noctem totam stertere:
ille opere foris faciendo lassus noctu ad me advenit;
fundum alienum arat, incultum familiarem deserit.
is etiam corruptus porro suom corrumpit filium.

row.cell: (too irate to notice unflattering accent) Yes, indeed! He busy in the Senate or helping his clients! He wearied out by his labours there, there, that he spends the whole night snoring! It is business away from home that makes him turn up at night all weary—the business of ploughing other people's fields and leaving his own uncultivated. Corrupt himself, he actually goes on and corrupts his own son.
Sequere hac me modo, iam faxo ipsum hominem manifesto opprimas.
Just follow me this way: I'll soon make you drop on our gentleman in the very act.
Nihil ecastor est quod facere mavelim.
Ah-h-h! There's nothing I'd like better!
Mane dum.
Hm! wait! (goes quietly to Cleareta's door, peeps in and comes back)
Quid est?
What's the matter?

cell.p: Possis, si forte accubantem tuom virum conspexeris
cum corona amplexum amicam, si videas, cognoscere?

row.cell: If you happened to spy your husband stretched out on a banquet couch with a garland on and a girl in his arms—if you saw him, could you recognize him?
Possum ecastor.
Indeed I can!
Em tibi hominem.
(taking her cautiously to the door) Behold your man!
Perii.
(peeping) Dreadful, dreadful!

cell.p: 880 Paulisper mane.
aucupemus ex insidiis clanculum quam rem gerant.

row.cell: (drawing her aside) Wait a bit! Let's lie in ambush and spy what's going on without being seen.
Quid modi, pater, amplexando facies?
(resentfully) Father! When is that hug going to end?
Fateor, gnate mi—
(somewhat embarrassed) I admit, my dear boy,—
Quid fatere?
Admit what?
Me ex amore huius corruptum oppido.
That this lady is altogether too much for my sense of decorum.
Audin quid ait?
(to Artemona) Do you hear what he says?
Audio.
I hear!

cell.p: Egon ut non domo uxori meae
subripiam in deliciis pallam quam habet, atque ad te deferam?
non edepol conduci possum vita uxoris annua.

row.cell: (to Philaenium) Not steal my wife's pet mantle from home and bring it to you? By heaven, I couldn't be hired not to—not if she should die within the year.
Censen tu illum hodie primum ire adsuetum esse in ganeum?
(to Artemona) Do you think to-day is the first time that gentleman has used such resorts?

cell.p: Ille ecastor suppilabat me, quod ancillas meas
suspicabar atque insontis miseras cruciabam.

row.cell: Mercy on us! So he was the thief all those times I suspected my maids, yes, and tortured the poor innocent things.

cell.p: Pater,
890 iube dari vinum; iam dudum factum est cum primum bibi.

row.cell: Tell them to set the wine going, father; it seems an age since I had my first drink.
Da, puere, ab summo. age, tu interibi ab infimo da savium.
(to servant) Boy, send round the wine from the head of the table. (to Philaenium) Come, my dear, meanwhile you send round a naughty, naughty kiss from the foot. (Philaenium obeys)
Perii misera, ut osculatur carnufex, capuli decus.
Oh-h-h! Good heavens! The way he kisses, the villain, fit only to grace a coffin!
Edepol animam suaviorem aliquanto quam uxoris meae.
My word! Rather sweeter breath than my wife's!
Dic amabo, an fetet anima uxoris tuae?
Do tell me, there's a dear—your wife's breath isn't bad, is it?

cell.p: Nauteam
bibere malim, si necessum sit, quam illam oscularier.

row.cell: I'd rather drink bilge water, if it came to that, than kiss her.

cell.p: Ain tandem? edepol ne tu istuc cum malo magno tuo
dixisti in me. sine, revenias modo domum, faxo ut scias
quid pericli sit dotatae uxori vitium dicere.

row.cell: (aside) So? You would, would you? Good gracious, sir, that fling at me will cost you dear. Very well! just you come back home, sir! I'll show you the danger of vilifying a wife with money.
Miser ecastor es.
Goodness me, you poor thing!
Ecastor dignus est.
(aside) Goodness me, he deserves to be!

cell.p: Quid ais, pater?
ecquid matrem amas?

row.cell: Look here, father. Do you love my mother?
900 Egone illam? nunc amo, quia non adest.
Love her? I? I love her now for not being near.
Quid cum adest?
And when she is near?
Periisse cupio.
I yearn for a death in the family.
Amat homo hic te, ut praedicat.
(to Artemona) This gentleman is fond of you, it seems.

cell.p: Ne illa ecastor faenerato funditat: nam si domum
redierit hodie. osculando ego ulciscar potissimum.

row.cell: (aside) Oh-h-h! won't he pay interest on that flow of words! Just let him come back home to-day, and that will be my favourite method of revenge—kissing him.
Iace, pater, talos, ut porro nos iaciamus.
(pushing some dice toward Demaenetus) Your throw, father: come, so that I can take my turn.

cell.p: Maxime.
te, Philaenium, mihi atque uxoris mortem, hoc Venerium est.
pueri, plaudite et mi ob iactum cantharo mulsum date.

row.cell: By all means. (as he throws) Here's to you for me, Philaenium, and my wife for the tomb! (looking at throw) Ha! The Venus!F (to servants) A cheer, lads, and some mead from the tankard for that throw!
Non queo durare.
(aside to Parasite) This is intolerable!

cell.p: Si non didicisti fulloniam,
non mirandum est.31 in oculos invadi optumum est.

row.cell: (aside to Artemona) No wonder, if you never learned the fuller'sG trade. Your best plan is to make a dash for his eyes.

cell.p: Ego pol vivam et tu istaec hodie cum tuo magno
malo invocavisti.

row.cell: (bursting into house) My heavens, sir, I will live, and you shall pay dear for that petition of yours just now! (tableau)
910 Ecquis currit pollictorem accersere?
(gleefully) Run, some one, and fetch the undertaker!
Mater, salve.
(innocently) How do you do, mother?
Sat salutis.
Enough of your how d'ye do-ing!

cell.p: Mortuost Demaenetus.
tempus est subducere hinc me; pulchre hoc gliscit proelium.
ibo ad Diabolum, mandata dicam facta ut voluerit,
atque interea ut decumbamus suadebo, hi dum litigant.

row.cell: (aside) Demaenetus is dead. Time for me to retire from the scene; the battle waxes finely. I'll off to Diabolus and tell him his mandates are executed to the letter, yes, and suggest our taking dinner meantime, while they fight it out.

cell.p: poste demum huc cras adducam ad lenam, ut viginti minas
ei det, in partem hac amanti ut liceat ei potirier.
Argyrippus exorari spero poterit, ut sinat
sese alternas cum illo noctes hac frui. nam ni impetro,
regem perdidi: ex amore tantum est homini incendium.

row.cell:
Then to-morrow when it's over I'll bring him back to the Madame so that he may give her the eighty pounds and get her permission for his fond self to go shares in the girl here. I do hope Argyrippus can be induced to let him have her half the time. For if I don't get so much out of him, I have lost a patron—all one blaze of love, as the fellow is.
[exit Parasite.
Quid tibi hunc receptio ad te est meum virum?
(to Philaenium) What do you mean by receiving this man at your house—my husband?

cell.p: 920 Pol me quidem
miseram odio enicavit.

row.cell: Dear, dear! Why, I'm fairly bored to death by him, for my part.
Surge, amator, i domum.
(standing over Demaenetus) Get up, my gallant; home with you!
Nullus sum.
(half aside, afraid to move) I'm a dead man!

cell.p: Immo es, ne nega, omnium unus pol nequissimus.
at etiam cubat cuculus. surge amator, i domum.

row.cell: Good gracious, no! You're the vilest man living, and you needn't deny it. But he's roosting there still, the cuckoo! Get up, my gallant; home with you!
Vae mihi.
(half aside) Oh, I'm in for it!
Vera hariolare. surge, amator, i domum.
You are a true prophet. Get up, my gallant; home with you!
Abscede ergo paululum istuc.
Well then, do stand a bit farther off.
Surge, amator, i domum.
Get up, my gallant; home with you!
Iam obsecro, uxor.
For heaven's sake now, my dear!

cell.p: Nunc uxorem me esse meministi tuam?
modo, cum dicta in me ingerebas, odium, non uxor eram.

row.cell: Now you recollect that I am your dear, do you? A moment ago, when you were saying things about me, I was your abomination, not your dear.
Totus perii.
(half aside) It's all up with me, absolutely!
Quid tandem? anima fetetne uxoris tuae?
You really meant it, did you? Your dear's breath smells, does it?
Murram olet.
(hastily) Smells of myrrh, myrrh!
Iam subrupuisti pallam, quam scorto dares?
(ironically) Have you stolen the mantle yet to give this creature?
930 Ecastor qui subrupturum pallam promisit tibi.
He promised he would steal it from you, indeed he did!
Non taces?
(aside to Philaenium) Shut up, won't you?
Ego dissuadebam, mater.
I tried to dissuade him, mother.

cell.p: Bellum filium.
istoscine patrem aequom est mores liberis largirier?
nilne te pudet?

row.cell: A pretty son! (to Demaenetus) Is this the way for a father to edify his children? Is there nothing you're ashamed of? (helps him off the couch by the ear)
Pol, si aliud nil sit, tui me, uxor, pudet.
Oh Lord! You make me ashamed, my dear, if nothing else would.
Cano capite te cuculum uxor ex lustris rapit.
(guiding him toward the door) It's your dear that is dragging you from this den of vice, your hoary-headed cuckoo!
Non licet manere—cena coquitur—dum cenem modo?
Mayn't I stay—dinner's being cooked—just till I've dined?
Ecastor cenabis hodie, ut dignus es, magnum malum.
Good heavens, sir! You shall dine as you deserve today—on dire distress.
Male cubandum est: iudicatum me uxor abducit domum.
(aside) It's a poorish night I'm in for: here I am sentenced, and my wife leading me off—home. (Argyrippus and Philaenium follow them to door)
Dicebam, pater, tibi, ne matri consuleres male.
I kept telling you, father, not to play any tricks on mother.
De palla memento, amabo.
Remember about the mantle, there's a dear!
Iuben hanc hinc abscedere?
(to wife) Tell her to get out of here, won't you?
I domum.
(jerking him along) Home with you!
940 Da savium etiam prius quam abis.
Do give me another naughty, naughty kiss before we part.
I in crucem.
Go to hell!
Immo intro potius. sequere hac me, mi anime.
Oh no, inside, instead, (to Argyrippus, as she goes back inside) Come along with me, darling.
Ego vero sequor.

Indeed I will.
[exeunt omnes.
GREX
EPILOGUE
(Spoken by the Company)

cell.p: Hic senex si quid clam uxorem suo animo fecit volup,
neque novum neque mirum fecit nec secus quam alii solent;
nec quisquam est tam ingenio duro nec tam firmo pectore,
quin ubi quicque occasionis sit sibi faciat bene.
nunc si voltis deprecari huic seni ne vapulet,
remur impetrari posse, plausum si clarum datis.

row.cell: If this old gentleman has indulged his inclinations a bit without informing his wife, he has done nothing new or strange, or different from what other men ordinarily do. No one has such an iron nature, such an unyielding heart, as not to do himself a good turn whenever he has any chance. So now in case you wish to beg the old fellow off from a beating, we opine that you can succeed, if you—give us some loud applause.

cell.p: 1. Leo brackets following v., 25-26:

p.hi: ita me obstinate adgressu's, ut non audeam
profecto, percontanti quin promam omnia.

row.cell: A. Where he might be beaten with ox-hide whips.

cell.p: 2. Leo brackets following v., 33:

p.hi: ubi flent nequam homines, qui polentam pinsitant.

row.cell: B. It has seemed advisable to use the terms of the English coinage system throughout this version; the value of the money metals, however, has shrunk very considerably since Plautus's day.
3. Corrupt (Leo): obsequellam MSS: obsequellam eam Acidalius.
C. The elm corresponded to our birch in being used for corporal punishment.

cell.p: 4. Leo brackets following v., 77:

p.hi: volo amori obsecutum illius, volo amet me patrem.

row.cell: D. White horses were supposed to be the fastest.
5. Corrupt (Leo): venari autem rete iaculo MSS: reti, iaculo venari autem Vahlen.
E. Naming one's sweetheart, on making a throw, was a common custom.
6. Leo notes lacuna here: atqui ibi MSS: ibo atque ibi Camerarius.
F. The highest throw.
7. Corrupt (Leo): experiri MSS: experi Skutsch.
G. Fullers being accustomed to unpleasant smells.

cell.p: 8. Leo brackets following v., 252:

p.hi: igitur inveniundo argento ut fingeres fallaciam.

row.cell: 9. Leo notes lacuna here: istuc MSS: istuc, istuc Palmer.
10. Corrupt (Leo): exasciato Acidalius: exasceatum MSS.
11. Leo notes lacuna here: da MSS: dare Fleckeisen.

cell.p: 12. Leo brackets following vv., 480-483:

p.hi: in ius voco te.

cell.p: Leon.

p.hi: Non eo.

cell.p: Merc.

p.hi: Non is? memento.

cell.p: Leon.
480 Memini.
Merc.

p.hi: Dabitur pol supplicum mihi de tergo vostro.

cell.p: Leon.

p.hi: Vae te
tibi quidem supplicum, carnufex de nobis detur?

cell.p: Merc.

p.hi: Atque etiam
pro dictis vostris maledicis poenae pendentur mi hodie.

row.cell: 13. etiam nunc dico MSS: Lindsay excises nunc dico.

row.cell: ARGVMENTVM I
ARGUMENT OF THE PLAY (I)

cell.p: Senex avarus vix sibi credens Euclio
domi suae defossam multis cum opibus
aulam invenit, rursumque penitus conditam
exanguis amens servat. eius filiam
Lyconides vitiarat. interea senex
Megadorus a sorore suasus ducere
uxorem avari gnatam deposcit sibi.

row.cell: A miserly old man named Euclio, a man who would hardly trust his very self, on finding a pot full of treasure buried within his house, hides it away again deep in the ground, and, beside himself with terror, keeps watch over it. His daughter had been wronged by Lyconides. Meanwhile an old gentleman, one Megadorus, is persuaded by his sister to marry, and asks the miser for his daughter's hand.

cell.p: durus senex vix promittit, atque aulae timens
domo sublatam variis abstrudit locis.
insidias servos facit huius Lyconidis
10 qui virginem vitiarat; atque ipse obsecrat
avonculum Megadorum sibimet cedere
uxorem amanti. per dolum mox Euclio
cum perdidisset aulam, insperato invenit
laetusque natam conlocat Lyconidi.

row.cell: The dour old fellow at length consents, and, fearing for his pot, takes it from the house and hides it in one place after another. The servant of this Lyconides, the man who had wronged the girl, plots against the miser; and Lyconides himself entreats his uncle, Megadorus, to give up the girl, and let him, the man that loves her, marry her. After a time Euclio, who had been tricked out of his pot, recovers it unexpectedly and joyfully bestows his daughter upon Lyconides.
ARGVMENTVM II
ARGUMENT OF THE PLAY (II)

cell.p: Aulam repertam auri plenam Euclio
Vi summa servat, miseris adfectus modis.
Lyconides istius vitiat filiam.
Volt hanc Megadorus indotatam ducere,
Lubensque ut faciat dat coquos cum obsonio.
Auro formidat Euclio, abstrudit foris.
Re omni inspecta compressoris servolus
Id surpit. illic Euclioni rem refert.
Ab eo donatur auro, uxore et filio.

row.cell: Euclio, on finding a pot full of gold, is dreadfully worried, and watches over it with the greatest vigilance. Lyconides wrongs his daughter. This girl, undowered though she is, Megadorus wishes to marry, and he cheerfully supplies cooks and provisions for the wedding feast. Anxious about his gold, Euclio hides it outside the house. Everything he does having been witnessed, a rascally servant of the girl's assailant steals it. His master informs Euclio of it, and receives from him gold, wife, and son.

TIBICINAE

cell.p: THE HOUSEHOLD GOD OF EUCLIO, the Prologue.
EUCLIO, an old gentleman of Athens.
STAPHYLA, his old slave.
EUNOMIA, a lady of Athens.
MEGADORUS, an old gentleman of Athens, Eunomia's brother.
PYTHODICUS, his slave.
CONGRIO, cook.
ANTHRAX, cook.
STROBILUS, slave of Lyconides.
LYCONIDES, a young gentleman of Athens, Eunomia's son.
PHAEDRIA, Euclio's daughter.
MUSIC GIRLS.

cell.hi: Scene—Athens. A street on which are the houses of Euclio and Megadorus, a narrow lane between them, in front an altar.

row.cell: PROLOGVS
PROLOGUE
LAR FAMILIARIS
SPOKEN BY EUCLIO'S HOUSEHOLD GOD

cell.p: Ne quis miretur qui sim, paucis eloquar
ego Lar sum familiaris ex hac familia
unde exeuntem me aspexistis. hanc domum
iam multos annos est cum possideo et colo
patri avoque iam huius qui nunc hic habet
sed mi avos huius obsecrans concredidit
thensaurum auri clam omnis. in medio foco
defodit, venerans me ut id servarem sibi.

row.cell: That no one may wonder who I am, I shall inform you briefly. I am the Household God of that family from whose house you saw me come. For many years now I have possessed this dwelling, and preserved it for the sire and grandsire of its present occupant. Now this man's grandsire as a suppliant entrusted to me, in utter secrecy, a hoard of gold: he buried it in the centre of the hearth, entreating me to guard it for him.

cell.p: is quoniam moritur—ita avido ingenio fuit—
10 numquam indicare id filio voluit suo,
inopemque optavit potius eum relinquere,
quam eum thensaurum commonstraret filio;
agri reliquit ei non magnum modum,
quo cum labore magno et misere viveret.

row.cell: When he died he could not bear—so covetous was he—to reveal its existence to his own son, and he chose to leave him penniless rather than apprise him of this treasure. Some land, a little only, he did leave him, whereon to toil and moil for a miserable livelihood.

cell.p: Ubi is obiit mortem qui mihi id aurum credidit,
coepi observare, ecqui maiorem filus
mihi honorem haberet quam eius habuisset pater.
atque ille vero minus minusque impendio
curare minusque me impertire honoribus.
20 item a me contra factum est, nam item obiit diem.
is ex se hunc reliquit qui hic nunc habitat filium
pariter moratum ut pater avosque huius fuit.

row.cell: After the death of him who had committed the gold to my keeping, I began to observe whether the son would hold me in greater honour than his father had. As a matter of fact, his neglect grew and grew apace, and he showed me less honour. I did the same by him: so he also died. He left a son who occupies this house at present, a man of the same mould as his sire and grandsire.

cell.p: huic filia una est. ea mihi cottidie
aut ture aut vino aut aliqui semper supplicat,
dat mihi coronas. eius honoris gratia
feci, thensaurum ut hic reperiret Euclio,
quo illam facilius nuptum, si vellet, daret
nam eam compressit de summo adulescens loco.
is scit adulescens quae sit quam compresserit,
30 illa illum nescit, neque compressam autem pater.

row.cell: He has one daughter. She prays to me constantly, with daily gifts of incense, or wine, or something; she gives me garlands. Out of regard for her I caused Euclio to discover the treasure here in order that he might the more easily find her a husband, if he wished. For she has been ravished by a young gentleman of very high rank. He knows who it is that he has wronged; who he is she does not know, and as for her father, he is ignorant of the whole affair.

cell.p: Eam ego hodie faciam ut his senex de proxumo
sibi uxorem poscat. id ea faciam gratia,
quo ille eam facilius ducat qui compresserat.
et hic qui poscet eam sibi uxorem senex,
is adulescentis illius est avonculus,
qui illam stupravit noctu, Cereris vigiliis.

row.cell: I shall make the old gentleman who lives next door here (pointing) ask for her hand to-day. My reason for so doing is that the man who wronged her may marry her the more easily. And the old gentleman who is to ask for her hand is the uncle of the young gentleman who violated her by night at the festival of Ceres.

cell.p: sed hic senex iam clamat intus ut solet.
anum foras extrudit, ne sit conscia.
credo aurum inspicere volt, ne subreptum siet.

row.cell:
(an uproar in Euclio's house) But there is old Euclio clamouring within as usual, and turning his ancient servant out of doors lest she learn his secret. I suppose he wishes to look at his gold and see that it is not stolen.
[exit.
ACTVS I
ACT I

cell.p: 40 Exi, inquam. age exi. exeundum hercle tibi hinc est foras,
circumspectatrix cum oculis emissicus.

row.cell:
(within) Out with you, I say! Come now, out with you! By the Lord, you've got to get out of here, you snook- around, you, with your prying and spying.
enter Staphyla from Euclio's house, followed by Euclio who is pushing and beating her.
Nam cur me miseram verberas?
(groaning) Oh, what makes you go a-hitting a poor wretch like me, sir?

cell.p: Ut misera sis
atque ut te dignam mala malam aetatem exigas.

row.cell: (savagely) To make sure you are a poor wretch, so as to give a bad lot the bad time she deserves.
Nam qua me nunc causa extrusisti ex aedibus?
Why, what did you push me out of the house for now?

cell.p: Tibi ego rationem reddam, stimulorum seges?
illuc regredere ab ostio. illuc sis vide,
ut incedit. at scin quo modo tibi res se habet?
si hercle hodie fustem cepero aut stimulum in manum,
testudineum istum tibi ego grandibo gradum.

row.cell: I give my reasons to you, you,—you patch of beats, you? Over there with you, (pointing) away from the door! (Staphyla hobbles to place indicated) Just look at her, will you,—how she creeps along! See here, do you know what'11 happen to you? Now by heaven, only let me lay my hand on a club or a stick and I'll accelerate that tortoise crawl for you!

cell.p: 50 Utinam me divi adaxint ad suspendium
potius quidem quam hoc pacto apud te servium.

row.cell: (aside) Oh, I wish Heaven would make me hang myself, I do! Better that than slaving it for you at this rate, I'm sure.

cell.p: At ut scelesta sola secum murmurat
oculos hercle ego istos, improba, ecfodiam tibi,
ne me observare possis quid rerum geram
abscede etiam nunc—etiam nunc—etiam—ohe.

row.cell: (aside) Hear the old criminal mumbling away to herself, though! (aloud) Ah! those eyes of yours, you old sinner! By heaven, I'll dig 'em out for you. I will, so that you can't keep watching me whatever I do. Get farther off still! still farther! still—Whoa!

cell.p: istic astato. si hercle tu ex istoc loco
digitum transvorsum aut unguem latum excesseris
aut si respexis, donicum ego te iussero,
continuo hercle ego te dedam discipulam cruci.

row.cell: Stand there! You budge a finger's breadth a nail's breadth from that spot; you so much as turn your head till I say the word, and by the Almighty, the next minute I'll send you to the gallows for a lesson, so I will.

cell.p: 60 scelestiorem me hac anu certo scio
vidisse numquam, nimisque ego hanc metuo male,
ne mi ex insidiis verba imprudent duit
neu persentiscat aurum ubi est absconditum,
quae in occipitio quoque habet oculos pessima.
nunc ibo ut visam sitne ita aurum ut condidi,
quod me sollicitat plurimis miserum modis.

row.cell: (aside) A worse reprobate than this old crone I never did see, no, never. Oh, but how horribly scared I am she'll come some sly dodge on me when I'm not expecting it, and smell out the place where the gold is hidden. She has eyes in the very back of her head, the hell-cat. Now I'll just go see if the gold is where I hid it. Dear, dear, it worries the life out of me! [exit Euclio into house.

cell.p: Noenum mecastor quid ego ero dicam meo
malae rei evenisse quamve insaniam,
queo comminisci; ita me miseram ad hunc modum
70 decies die uno saepe extrudit aedibus.
nescio pol quae illunc hominem intemperiae tenent;
pervigilat noctes totas, tum autem interdius
quasi claudus sutor domi sedet totos dies.

row.cell: Mercy me! What's come over master, what crazy streak he's got, I can't imagine,—driving a poor woman out of the house this way ten times a day, often. Goodness gracious, what whim-whams the man's got into his head I don't see. Never shuts his eyes all night: yes, and then in the daytime he's sitting around the house the whole livelong day, for all the world like a lame cobbler.

cell.p: neque iam quo pacto celem erilis filiae
probrum, propinqua partitudo cui appetit,
queo comminisci; neque quicquam meliust mihi,
ut opinor, quam ex me ut unam faciam litteram
longam, meum laqueo collum quando obstrinxero.

row.cell: How I'm going to hide the young mistress's disgrace now is beyond me, and she with her time so near. There's nothing better for me to do, as I see, than tie a rope round my neck and dangle myself out into one long capital I.
Scene 2.
re-enter Euclio from house.

cell.p: Nunc defaecato demum animo egredior domo,
80 postquam perspexi salva esse intus omnia.
redi nunciam intro atque intus serva.

row.cell: (aside) At last I can feel easy about leaving the house, now I have made certain everything is all right inside. (to Staphyla) Go back in there this instant, you, and keep watch inside.

cell.p: Quippini?
ego intus servem? an ne quis aedes auferat?
nam hic apud nos nihil est aliud quaesti furibus,
ita inaniis sunt oppletae atque araneis.

row.cell: (tartly) I suppose so! So I'm to keep watch inside, am I? You aren't afraid anyone'll walk away with the house, are you? I vow we've got nothing else there for thieves to take—all full of emptiness as it is, and cobwebs.

cell.p: Mirum quin tua me causa faciat Iuppiter
Philippum regem aut Dareum, trivenefica
araneas mihi ego illas servari volo.
pauper sum, fateor, patior, quod di dant fero.

row.cell: It is surprising Providence wouldn't make a King Philip or Darius of me for your benefit, you viper, you! (threateningly) I want those cobwebs watched! I'm poor, poor; I admit it, I put up with it; I take what the gods give me.

cell.p: abi intro, occlude ianuam. iam ego hic ero
90 cave quemquam alienum in aedis intro miseris
quod quispiam ignem quaerat, extingui volo,
ne causae quid sit quod te quisquam quaeritet
nam si ignis vivet, ut extinguere extempulo.

row.cell: In with you, bolt the door. I shall be back soon. No outsider is to be let in, mind you. And in case anyone should be looking for a light, see you put the fire out so that no one will have any reason to come to you for it. Mark my words, if that fire stays alive, I'll extinguish you instantly.

cell.p: tum aquam aufugisse dicito, si quis petet.
cultrum, securim, pistillum, mortarium,
quae utenda vasa semper vicini rogant,
fures venisse atque abstulisse dicito
profecto in aedis meas me absente neminem
volo intro mitti. atque etiam hoc praedico tibi
100 si Bona Fortuna veniat, ne intro miseris

row.cell: And then water—if anyone asks for water, tell him it's all run out. As for a knife, or an axe, or a pestle, or a mortar,—things the neighbours are all the time wanting to borrow—tell 'em burglars got in and stole the whole lot. I won't have a living soul let into my house while I'm gone—there! Yes, and what's more, listen here, if Dame Fortune herself comes along, don't you let her in.

cell.p: Pol ea ipsa credo ne intro mittatur cavet,
nam ad aedis nostras numquam adit, quamquam prope est.

row.cell: Goodness me, she won't get in: she'll see to that herself, I fancy. Why, she never comes to our house at all, no matter how near she is.
Tace atque abi intro.
Keep still and go inside. (advances on her)
Taceo atque abeo.
(hurrying out of reach) I'm still, sir, I'm going!

cell.p: Occlude sis
fores ambobus pessulis. iam ego hic ero.

row.cell:
Mind you lock the door, both bolts. I'll soon be back.
[exit Staphyla into house.

cell.p: discrucior animi, quia ab domo abeundum est mihi.
nimis hercle invitus abeo. sed quid agam scio.
nam noster nostrae qui est magister curiae
dividere argenti dixit nummos in viros,
id si relinquo ac non peto, omnes ilico
110 me suspicentur, credo habere aurum domi
nam non est veri simile, hominem pauperem
pauxillum parvi facere quin nummum petat.

row.cell: It's agony having to leave the house, downright agony. Oh my God, how I do hate to go! But I have my reasons. The director of our ward gave notice he was going to make us a present of two shillings a man; and the minute I let it pass without putting in my claim, they'd all be suspecting I had gold at home, I'm sure they would. No, it doesn't look natural for a poor man to think so little of even a tiny bit of money as not to go ask for his two shillings.

cell.p: nam nunc cum celo sedulo omnis, ne sciant,
omnes videntur scire et me benignius
omnes salutant quam salutabant prius;
adeunt, consistunt, copulantur dexteras,
rogitant me ut valeam, quid agam, quid rerum geram.
nunc quo profectus sum ibo; postidea domum
me rursum quantum potero tantum recipiam.

row.cell:
Why, even now, hard as I try to keep every one from finding out, it seems as if every one knew: it seems as if every one has a heartier way of saying good day than they used to. Up they come, and stop, and shake hands, and keep asking me how I'm feeling, and how I'm getting on, and what I'm doing. Well, I must get along to where I'm bound; and then I'll come back home just as fast as I possibly can.
[exit Euclio.
ACTVS II
ACT II
enter Eunomia and Megadorus from latter's house.

cell.p: 120 Velim te arbitrari med haec verba, frater,
meai fidei tuaique rei
causa facere, ut aequom est germanam sororem.
quamquam haud falsa sum nos odiosas haberi;
nam multum loquaces merito omnes habemur,
nec mutam profecto repertam ullam esse
aut hodie dicunt mulierem aut ullo in saeclo.

row.cell: Brother, I do hope you'll believe I say this out of my loyalty to you and for your welfare, as a true sister should. Of course I'm well enough aware you men think us women are a bother; yes, awful chatterboxes—that's the name we all have, and (ruefully) it fits. And then that common saying, "Never now, nor through the ages, never any woman dumb."

cell.p: verum hoc, frater, unum tamen cogitato,
tibi proximam me mihique esse item te;
ita aequom est quod in rem esse utrique arbitremur
130 et mihi te et tibi me consulere et monere;
neque occultum id haberi neque per metum mussari,
quin participem pariter ego te et tu me ut facias,
eo nunc ego secreto ted huc foras seduxi,
ut tuam rem ego tecum hic loquerer familiarem.

row.cell: But just the same, do remember this one thing, brother,—that I am closer to you and you to me than anyone else in the whole world. So both of us ought to advise and counsel each other as to what we feel is to either's advantage, not keep such things back or be afraid to speak out openly, we ought to confide in one another fully, you and I. This is why I've taken you aside out here now—so that we can have a quiet talk on a matter that concerns you intimately.
Da mi, optuma femina, manum.
(warmly) Let's have your hand, you best of women!
Ubi ea est? quis ea est nam optuma?
(pretending to look about) Where is she? Who on earth is that best of women?
Tu.
Yourself.
Tune ais?
You say that—you?
Si negas, nego.
(banteringly) Oh well, if you deny it—

cell.p: Decet te equidem vera proloqui;
nam optuma nulla potest eligi:
alia alia peior, frater, est.

row.cell: Really now, you ought to be truthful. There's no such thing, you know, as picking out the best woman; it's only a question of comparative badness, brother.

cell.p: 140 Idem ego arbitror,
nec tibi advorsari certum est de istac re umquam, soror.

row.cell: My own opinion precisely. I'll never differ with you there, sister, you may count on that.
Da mihi operam amabo.
Now do give me your attention, there's a dear.
Tuast, utere atque impera, si quid vis.
It is all your own; use me, command me—anything you wish.
Id quod in rem tuam optumum esse arbitror, ted id monitum advento.
I'm going to advise you to do something that I think will be the very best thing in the world for you.
Soror, more tuo facis.
Quite like you, sister.
Factum volo.
I certainly hope so.
Quid est id, soror?
And what is this something, my dear?

cell.p: Quod tibi sempiternum
salutare sit: liberis procreandis—
ita di faxint—volo te uxorem
domum ducere.

row.cell: Something that will make for your everlasting welfare. You should have children. God grant you may!—and I want you to marry.
Ei occidi.
Oh-h-h, murder!
150 Quid ita?
How so?

cell.p: Quia mihi misero cerebrum excutiunt
tua dicta, soror: lapides loqueris.

row.cell: Well, you're knocking my poor brains out with such a proposition, my dear girl: you're talking cobble-stones.
Heia, hoc face quod te iubet soror.
Now, now, do what your sister tells you.
Si lubeat, faciam.
I would, if it appealed to me.
In rem hoc tuam est.
It would be a good thing for you.

cell.p: Ut quidem emoriar prius quam ducam.
sed his legibus si quam dare vis ducam:
quae cras veniat, perendie foras feratur;
his legibus dare vis? cedo: nuptias adorna.

row.cell: Yes—to die before marrying. (pause) All right. I'll marry anyone you please, on this condition, though: her wedding to-morrow, and her wake the day after. Still wish it, on this condition? Produce her! Arrange for the festivities!

cell.p: Cum maxima possum tibi, frater, dare dote;
sed est grandior natu: media est mulieris aetas.
160 eam si iubes, frater, tibi me poscere, poscam.

row.cell: I can get you one with ever so big a dowry, dear. To be sure, she's not a young girl—middle-aged, as a matter of fact. I'll see about it for you, brother, if you want.
Num non vis me interrogare te?
You don't mind my asking you a question, I dare say?
Immo, si quid vis, roga.
Why, of course not; anything you like.

cell.p: Post mediam aetatem qui media ducit uxorem domum,
si eam senex anum praegnatem fortuito fecerit,
quid dubitas, quin sit paratum nomen puero Postumus?

row.cell: Now supposing a man pretty well on in life marries a lady of maturity and this aged female should happen to show intentions of making the old fellow a father—can you doubt but that the name in store for that youngster is Postumus?A

cell.p: nunc ego istum, soror, laborem demam et deminuam tibi.
ego virtute deum et maiorum nostrum dives sum satis.
istas magnas factiones, animos, dotes dapsiles,
clamores, imperia, eburata vehicla, pallas, purpuram,
nil moror quae in servitutem sumptibus redigunt viros.

row.cell: See here, sister, I'll relieve you of all this and save you trouble. I'm rich enough, thanks be to heaven and our forbears. And I have no fancy at all for those ladies of high station and hauteur and fat dowries, with their shouting and their ordering and their ivory trimmed carriages and their purple and fine linen that cost a husband his liberty.
Dic mihi, quaeso, quis ea est quam vis ducere uxorem?
For mercy's sake tell me who you do want to marry, then!

cell.p: 170 Eloquar.
nostin hunc senem Euclionem ex proximo pauperculum?

row.cell: I'm going to. You know the old gentleman—rather hard up, poor fellow,—that lives next door, Euclio?
Novi, hominem haud malum mecastor.
Yes indeed. Why, he seems quite nice.

cell.p: Eius cupio filiam
virginem mihi desponderi. verba ne facias, soror.
scio quid dictura es: hanc esse pauperem. haec pauper placet.

row.cell: It's his daughter—there's the engagement I'm eager for. Now don't make a fuss, sister. I know what you're about to say—that she's poor. But this particular poor girl suits me.
Di bene vortant.
God's blessing on your choice, dear!
Idem ego spero.
I trust so.
Quid me? num quid vis?
(about to leave) Well, there's nothing I can do?
Vale.
Yes—take good care of yourself.
Et tu, frater.

You too, brother.
[exit Eunomia.

cell.p: Ego conveniam Euclionem, si domi est.
sed eccum video. nescio unde sese homo recipit domum.

row.cell: Now for an interview with Euclio, if he's at home. (looking down street) Hullo, though! here he is! Just getting back from somewhere or other.
II. 2.
Scene 2.
enter Euclio.

cell.p: Praesagibat mi animus frustra me ire, quom exibam domo;
itaque abibam invitus; nam neque quisquam curialium
180 venit neque magister quem dividere argentum oportuit.
nunc domum properare propero, nam egomet sum hic, animus domi est.

row.cell: (without seeing Megadorus) I knew it! Something told me I was going on a fool's errand when I left the house; that's why I hated to go. Why, there wasn't a single man of our ward there, or the director either, who ought to have distributed the money. Now I'll hurry up and hurry home: I'm here in the body, but that's where my mind is.
Salvos atque fortunatus, Euclio, semper sies.
(advancing with outstretched hand) Good day to you, Euclio, yes, and the best of everything to you always!
Di te ament, Megadore.
(taking hand gingerly) God bless you, Megadorus.
Quid tu? recten atque ut vis vales?
How goes it? All right, are you? Feeling as well as you could wish?

cell.p: Non temerarium est, ubi dives blande appellat pauperem.
iam illic homo aurum scit me habere, eo me salutat blandius.

row.cell: (aside) There's something behind it when a rich man puts on that smooth air with a poor one. Now that fellow knows I've got gold: that's why he's so uncommon smooth with his salutations.
Ain tu te valere?
You say you are well?
Pol ego haud perbene a pecunia.
Heavens, no: I feel low, very low—in funds.
Pol si est animus aequos tibi. sat habes qui bene vitam colas.
(cheerily) Well, well, man, if you have a contented mind, you've got enough to enjoy life with.

cell.p: Anus hercle huic indicium fecit de auro, perspicue palam est.
cui ego iam linguam praecidam atque oculos effodiam domi.

row.cell: (aside, frightened) Oh, good Lord! The old woman has let on to him about the gold! It's discovered, clear as can be! I'll cut her tongue out, I'll tear her eyes out, the minute I get at her in the house!
Quid tu solus tecum loquere?
What is that you're saying to yourself?

cell.p: 190 Meam pauperiem conqueror.
virginem habeo grandem, dote cassam atque inlocabilem,
neque eam queo locare cuiquam.

row.cell: (startled) Just ... how awful it is to be poor. And I with a grown-up girl, without a penny of dowry, that I can't get off my hands or find a husband for.

cell.p: Tace, bonum habe animum, Euclio.
dabitur, adiuvabere a me. dic, si quid opust, impera.

row.cell: (clapping him on the back) There, there, Euclio! Cheer up. She shall be married: I'll help you out. Come now, call on me, if you need anything.

cell.p: Nunc petit, cum pollicetur; inhiat aurum ut devoret.
altera manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera.
nemini credo qui large blandust dives pauperi
ubi manum inicit benigne, ibi onerat aliqua zamia
ego istos novi polypos, qui ubi quidquid tetigerunt tenent.

row.cell: (aside) When he agrees to give he wants to grab! Mouth wide open to gobble down my gold! Holds up a bit of bread in one hand and has a stone in the other! I don't trust one of these rich fellows when he's so monstrous civil to a poor man. They give you a cordial handshake, and squeeze something out of you at the same time. I know all about those octopuses that touch a thing and then—stick.

cell.p: Da mi operam parumper. paucis, Euclio, est quod te volo
de communi re appellare mea et tua.

row.cell: I should be glad to have a moment of your time, Euclio. I want to have a brief talk with you on a matter that concerns us both.

cell.p: 200 Ei misero mihi,
aurum mi intus harpagatum est. nunc hic eam rem volt scio,
mecum adire ad pactionem. verum intervisam domum.

row.cell: (aside) Oh, God save us! My gold's been hooked, and now he wants to make a deal with me! I see it all! But I'll go in and look. (hurries toward house)
Quo abis?
Where are you off to?
Iam ad te revortar. nunc est quod visam domum.

Just a moment!... I'll be back ... the fact is ... I must see to something at home.
[exit into house.

cell.p: Credo edepol, ubi mentionem ego fecero de filia
mi ut despondeat, sese a me derideri rebitur,
neque illo quisquam est alter hodie ex paupertate parcior.

row.cell:
By Jove! I suppose he'll think I'm making fun of him when I speak about his giving me his daughter; poverty never made a fellow closer-fisted.
re-enter Euclio.

cell.p: Di me servant, salva res est. salvom est si quid non perit
nimis male timui. prius quam intro redii, exanimatus fui.
redeo ad te, Megadore, si quid me vis.

row.cell: (aside) Thank the Lord, I'm saved! It's safe—that is, if it's all there. Ah, but that was a dreadful moment! I nearly expired before I got in the house. (to Megadorus) Here I am, Megadorus, if you want anything of me.

cell.p: Habeo gratiam.
210 quaeso, quod te percontabor, ne id te pigeat pro loqui.

row.cell: Thanks. Now I trust you won't mind answering the questions I'm going to ask.
Dum quidem ne quid perconteris quod non lubeat proloqui.
(cautiously) No-no—that is, if you don't ask any I don't like to answer.
Dic mihi. quali me arbitrare genere prognatum?
Frankly now, what do you think of my family connections?
Bono.
(grudgingly) Good.
Quid fide?
And my sense of honour?
Bona.
Good.
Quid factis?
And my general conduct?
Neque malis neque improbis.
Not bad, not disreputable.
Aetatem meam scis?
You know my age?
Scio esse grandem, item ut pecuniam.
Getting on, getting on, I know that—(aside) financially, too.

cell.p: Certe edepol equidem te civem sine mala omni malitia
semper sum arbitratus et nunc arbitror.

row.cell: Now Euclio, I've always considered you a citizen of the true, trusty type, by Jove, I certainly have, and I do still.

cell.p: Aurum huic olet.
quid nunc me vis?

row.cell: (aside) He's got a whiff of my gold. (aloud) Well, what do you want?

cell.p: Quoniam tu me et ego te qualis sis scio.
quae res recte vortat mihique tibique tuaeque filiae,
filiam tuam mi uxorem posco. promitte hoc fore.

row.cell: Now that we appreciate each other, I'm going to ask you—and may it turn out happily for you and your girl and me—to give me your daughter in marriage. Promise you will.

cell.p: 220 Heia, Megadore, haud decorum facinus tuis factis facis,
ut inopem atque innoxium abs te atque abs tuis me inrideas.
nam de te neque re neque verbis merui ut faceres quod facis.

row.cell: (whining) Now, now, Megadorus! This is unlike you, unworthy of you, making fun of a poor man like me that never harmed you or yours. Why, I never said or did a thing to you to deserve being treated so.

cell.p: Neque edepol ego te derisum venio neque derideo,
neque dignum arbitror.

row.cell: Good Lord, man! I didn't come here to make fun of you, and I'm not making fun of you: I couldn't think of such a thing.
Cur igitur poscis meam gnatam tibi?
Then why are you asking for my daughter?
Ut propter me tibi sit melius mihique propter te et tuos.
Why? So that we may all of us make life pleasanter for one another.

cell.p: Venit hoc mihi, Megadore, in mentem, ted esse hominem divitem,
factiosum, me autem esse hominem pauperum pauperrimum;
nunc si filiam locassim meam tibi, in mentem venit
te bovem esse et me esse asellum: ubi tecum coniunctus siem,
230 ubi onus nequeam ferre pariter, iaceam ego asinus in luto,
tu me bos magis haud respicias, gnatus quasi numquam siem.

row.cell: Now here's the way it strikes me, Megadorus,—you're a rich man, a man of position: but as for me, I'm poor, awfully poor, dreadfully poor. Now if I was to marry off my daughter to you, it strikes me you'd be the ox and I'd be the donkey. When I was hitched up with you and couldn't pull my share of the load, down I'd drop, I, the donkey, in the mud; and you, the ox, wouldn't pay any more attention to me than if I'd never been born at all.

cell.p: et te utar iniquiore et meus me ordo inrideat,
neutrubi habeam stabile stabulum, si quid divorti fuat:
asini me mordicibus scindant, boves incursent cornibus.
hoc magnum est periclum, ab asinis ad boves transcendere.

row.cell: You would be too much for me: and my own kind would haw-haw at me: and if there should be a falling out, neither party would let me have stable quarters: the donkeys would chew me up and the oxen would run me through. It is a very hazardous business for donkeys to climb into the ox set.

cell.p: Quam ad probos propinquitate proxime te adiunxeris.
tam optumum est. tu condicionem hanc accipe, ausculta mihi,
atque eam desponde mi.

row.cell: But honourable human beings—the more closely connected you are with them, the better. Come, come, accept my offer: listen to what I say and promise her to me.
At nihil est dotis quod dem.
But not one penny of dowry can I give.

cell.p: Ne duas.
dum modo morata recte veniat, dotata est satis.

row.cell: Don't. Only let me have a girl that's good, and she has dowry enough.
240 Eo dico, ne me thensauros repperisse censeas.
(forcing a laugh) I mention this just so that you mayn't think I've found some treasure.
Novi, ne doceas. desponde.
Yes, yes, I understand. Promise.

cell.p: Fiat. sed pro Iuppiter,
num ego disperii?

row.cell: So be it. (aside, starting at noise) Oh, my God! Can it be I'm ruined, ruined?
Quid tibi est?
What's the matter?
Quid crepuit quasi ferrum modo?

That noise? What was it—a sort of clinking sound?
[exit into house hurriedly.

cell.p: Hic apud me hortum confodere iussi. sed ubi hic est homo?
abiit neque me certiorem fecit. fastidit mei,
quia videt me suam amicitiam velle. more hominum facit;
nam si opulentus it petitum pauperioris gratiam,
pauper metuit congrediri, per metum male rem gerit.
idem, quando occasio illaec periit, post sero cupit.

row.cell:
(not noticing his departure) I told them to do some digging in my garden here. (looking around) But where is the man? Gone away and left me—without a word! Scorns me, now he sees I desire his friendship! Quite the usual thing, that. Yes, let a wealthy man try to get the regard of a poorer one, and the poor one is afraid to meet him half-way: his timidity makes him injure his own interests. Then when it's too late and the opportunity is gone he longs to have it again.
re-enter Euclio.

cell.p: 250 Si hercle ego te non elinguandam dedero usque ab radicibus,
impero auctorque ego sum, ut tu me cuivis castrandum loces.

row.cell: (to Staphyla within) By heaven, if I don't have your tongue torn out by the very roots, I give you orders, give you full authority, to hand me over to anyone you please to be skinned alive. (approaches Megadorus)

cell.p: Video hercle ego te me arbitrari, Euclio, hominem idoneum,
quem senecta aetate ludos facias, haud merito meo.

row.cell: Upon my word, Euclio! So you think I am the proper sort of man to make a fool of, at my time of life, and without the slightest reason.
Neque edepol, Megadore, facio, neque. si cupiam, copia est.
Bless my soul! I'm not making a fool of you, Megadorus: I couldn't if I would.
Quid nunc? etiam mihi despondes filiam?
(doubtfully) Well now, do you mean I am to have your daughter?

cell.p: Illis legibus,
cum illa dote quam tibi dixi.

row.cell: On the understanding she goes with the dowry I mentioned.
Sponden ergo?
You consent, then?
Spondeo.
I consent.
Di bene vertant.
And may God prosper us!

cell.p: Ita di faxint. illud facito ut memineris
convenisse ut ne quid dotis mea ad te afferret filia.

row.cell: Yes, yes,—and mind you remember our agreement about the dowry: she doesn't bring you a single penny.
Memini.
I remember.

cell.p: At scio quo vos soleatis pacto perplexarier.
260 pactum non pactum est, non pactum pactum est, quod vobis lubet.
